blocks.text: That they were immense in number, Moses proves by two arguments. The first is that they were scattered not only through the camp but on every side, for a day's journey, and stood two cubits high above the ground. The second is that so many myriads of men laboured for two whole days in catching and gathering them that he who had gathered the least of them heaped up ten cors [Numer. XI, 31. 32.]. This cloud of quails, then, extended on every side at least forty miles (for a day's journey is at least twenty miles), and rose two cubits above the ground. This can be understood in three ways. 1. That it means the quails were so heaped up over that whole space that everywhere they rose to two cubits. 2. That it signifies heaps of quails two cubits high, scattered here and there in such a way that empty spaces were left between them, through which the people might make their way to gather the food offered by God. 3. That it signifies that in their very flight they came down so low that they were no more than two cubits from the ground, as though offering themselves of their own accord to the hands of those catching them. Following this, Jerome rendered the sacred words thus: And they flew in the air at a height of two cubits above the ground. And Jonathan: וכרום תרתין אמין הוה פרח על אנפי ארעא והוו מהלכין בהון עד פרתהון מטול דלא ילעון בזמן מכנשהון יתהון, And they flew at a height of two cubits over the face of the ground, and (the Israelites) walked among them up to the navel, so that they might not toil in gathering them. And R. Selomo in his Notes: פורחות בגובה עד שהן כנגד לבו של אדם כדי שלא יהא טורח באסיפתן לא להגביה ולא לשחות, They flew at the height of a man's breast, so that no one in gathering them should tire himself by stretching up or bending down. Nor do I doubt that Philo had this very thing in mind when he describes ὀρτυγομητρῶν νέφος τὰς πτήσεις προσγειοτάτας ποιούμενον εἰς τὸ εὔθηρον [ortygomētrōn nephos tas ptēseis prosgeiotatas poioumenon eis to euthēron], a cloud of quails flying very close to the ground, so that catching them was easy. This fits the nature of the quail not badly, which, when it comes to us, says Pliny, is a ground bird rather than a high-flying one. I am therefore not averse to this interpretation, although I prefer the second, because David says expressly that the quails fell in the midst of the camp, and Moses that they were spread out upon the ground. These words seem to describe birds lying flat on the ground rather than fluttering in the lowest air. The word raining points the same way, for only things that fall all the way to the ground are said to rain. Moreover, had they been flying, hardly so many could have been caught in two days that each man had [II, 669] ten cors ^{(9)}. For the cor was the largest measure of the Hebrews, containing ten baths, as the bath contained three seahs, the seah six kabs, the kab four logs, the log six eggs. In Hebrew it is called חומר chomer, which some of the Hebrews derive from חמור chamor, that is, ass, as though it had been an ass's load. But others more correctly contend that the cor was twice as heavy, and so would have loaded a camel. It is therefore most probable that in the space Moses defines, that is, a day's journey around the camp, heaps of quails lay not everywhere but here and there ^{(10)}, in places rising two cubits above the ground. These, wearied by their long flight, either divine power, or angels sent by God, or rather violent winds had scattered hither and thither, to serve this people as food.
